# Raw Typst blocks

Markdown covers most needs, but sometimes you want direct control. A fenced
block marked `{=typst}` passes its contents *straight through* to the Typst
compiler:

````markdown
```{=typst}
#text(fill: red, weight: "bold")[This text is red and bold.]
```
````

Which produces:

```{=typst}
#text(fill: red, weight: "bold")[This text is red and bold.]
```

Two things to notice about Typst syntax:

- Functions start with `#`, e.g. `#text(...)`, and take options in `(...)`.
- Content goes in square brackets: `[like this]`.

# Styling with `#set` rules

A `#set` rule changes the default of a function *from that point onward*.
This paragraph break is followed by a set rule that enlarges paragraph
spacing and justifies text:

```{=typst}
#set par(justify: true)
```

From here on, all paragraphs are justified — note how the right-hand edge of
this paragraph is now perfectly flush, unlike the ragged paragraphs above.
Set rules are the workhorse of Typst styling: one line changes the whole
document from here down.

# Transforming with `#show` rules

A `#show` rule *transforms* elements. This one repaints every piece of
emphasised text in teal:

```{=typst}
#show emph: set text(fill: rgb("#1f6f8b"))
```

Now *any emphasised text* — written with ordinary Markdown asterisks — comes
out *teal*. Show rules let you restyle Markdown output without touching the
Markdown itself.

# Boxes and callouts, Typst-style

Typst's `#block` and `#rect` make attractive containers:

```{=typst}
#block(
  fill: rgb("#eef6f8"),
  stroke: (left: 3pt + rgb("#1f6f8b")),
  inset: 10pt,
  radius: 4pt,
  width: 100%,
)[
  *Key idea.* Use Markdown for content, raw Typst for presentation.
  Keep the two concerns separate and your documents stay maintainable.
]
```

Quarto's own callouts also work and are translated to Typst for you:

::: {.callout-note}
This is a standard Quarto callout. It renders natively in Typst — no extra
work needed.
:::

# Mixing R output with Typst

Important gotcha: inline R code is **not** evaluated inside a raw
`{=typst}` fence (knitr treats the fence as verbatim). The reliable pattern
is to *generate* the Typst code from an R chunk with `output: asis`:

```{r}
#| echo: fenced
#| output: asis
best <- rownames(mtcars)[which.max(mtcars$mpg)]
val  <- max(mtcars$mpg)

cat("```{=typst}\n",
    "#align(center)[",
    "#block(fill: rgb(\"#fff4e6\"), inset: 12pt, radius: 6pt)[",
    "#text(size: 20pt, weight: \"bold\")[", val, " mpg]\n\n",
    "Most efficient car in `mtcars`: ", best,
    "]]\n",
    "```", sep = "")
```

The chunk computes values in R, then `cat()`s a raw Typst block into the
document. Anything you can compute, you can typeset.

# Two-column sections

You can switch to multi-column layout mid-document:

```{=typst}
#columns(2)[
  #lorem(60)
]
```

(`#lorem(n)` generates *n* words of placeholder text — handy for layout
experiments.)

# Exercises

## 🏋️ Exercise 2.1 — Colour play

Add a raw Typst block that prints your name in 24pt, purple
(`rgb("#6a0dad")`), centred with `#align(center)[...]`.

## 🏋️ Exercise 2.2 — A show rule for strong text

Write a `#show strong: ...` rule so that all **bold Markdown text** below it
is rendered in small caps (`smallcaps`) — then write a bold sentence to
prove it works. Hint: `#show strong: it => smallcaps(it)`.

## 🏋️ Exercise 2.3 — Design a warning box

Build a "warning" box with `#block`: pale red fill (`rgb("#fdecea")`), a
3pt red left border, and inset of 10pt. Put a short warning about
overusing raw Typst inside it.

## 🏋️ Exercise 2.4 — Data-driven Typst

Using the `output: asis` pattern above, compute the mean of
`iris$Sepal.Length` in R and display it inside a centred Typst statistic
box like the mtcars example.
